overview: An everyday-language task is translated into route data (Routendaten), a precise requirement (präzise Anforderung), and an algorithm (Algorithmus). The goal is to find the fastest route without stairs. When durations are equal, the first route in the given order remains selected, as specified by the tie-breaking rule (Gleichstandsregel). If no route is suitable, the result is “No suitable route” (Keine geeignete Route). The algorithm keeps track of the best route seen so far and checks each new route once. With constant work per route, this takes Θ(n) work; rescanning all previous routes after each new route takes Θ(n²). Requirements, testing (Testen), and correctness (Korrektheit) must also be checked when using AI and implementing the solution in Java.

entries.short: A route is described by its identifier, duration, and whether it includes stairs.
entries.explanation: A program can compare routes only by their stored properties. To select the fastest route without stairs, it needs an identifier, a duration, and information about stairs.
entries.example: Route C can be described as “C, 9 minutes, no stairs.”
pitfalls: The route with the shortest duration is not necessarily suitable if it includes stairs.
entries.heading: Ein Ort wird zu Daten

entries.short: An ordered route list contains routes in a fixed order, which the algorithm follows when checking them.
entries.explanation: The input is a list of routes with an identifier, duration, and information about stairs. The order matters because, when durations are equal, the first suitable route is selected.
entries.example: In the list A, B, C, A comes before B, and B comes before C.
pitfalls: Changing the order before selection can change which route is selected in a tie.
entries.heading: Präzise Anforderung

entries.short: A precise requirement describes the input, the desired selection, how ties are handled, and the result when no route is suitable.
entries.explanation: The input is an ordered list of routes with an identifier, duration, and information about stairs. Select the fastest route without stairs; when durations are equal, keep the first route in the given order. If no route is suitable, report “No suitable route.” This specifies exactly what the program is supposed to do.
entries.example: For A (12 minutes, no stairs), B (7 minutes, with stairs), and C (9 minutes, no stairs), the desired selection is C.
pitfalls: “Find the best route” is imprecise unless “best” is defined.
A route with stairs must not be selected if the requirement excludes stairs.
entries.heading: Präzise Anforderung

entries.short: A route is suitable for this task if it has no stairs.
entries.explanation: Suitability is determined by the requirement and checked separately from duration. Only after identifying the suitable routes do we look for the fastest one.
entries.example: A route that takes 7 minutes and has stairs is unsuitable, even if it is faster than a route without stairs.
pitfalls: Duration alone does not determine suitability.
entries.heading: Übung: Regeln für beliebige Routenlisten formulieren

entries.short: The stairs filter ignores every route with stairs so that only suitable routes are compared.
entries.explanation: The filter implements the requirement “no stairs.” After filtering, only suitable routes are compared by duration. Check each route for stairs, ignore routes with stairs, and consider routes without stairs when making the selection.
entries.example: For A (12 minutes, no stairs), B (7 minutes, with stairs), and C (9 minutes, no stairs), B is ignored.
pitfalls: The filter does not allow a route with stairs as a fallback if no suitable route exists.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far (Algorithmus mit einer bisher besten Route)
entries.heading: Übung: Regeln für beliebige Routenlisten formulieren

entries.short: “No suitable route” is the result when no route satisfies the condition “no stairs.”
entries.explanation: The algorithm must handle this case explicitly; otherwise, it cannot produce a route. If the requirement stays unchanged, this message is a valid result.
entries.example: If A, B, and C all have stairs, the result is “No suitable route.”
pitfalls: If the requirement is unchanged, the fastest route with stairs must not simply be returned.
entries.heading: Sonderfall: Alle Routen enthalten Treppen

entries.short: A fallback rule that selects a route with stairs when no suitable route exists changes the requirement.
entries.explanation: One possible additional rule would be to select the fastest route with stairs if all routes have stairs. This contradicts the original condition “no stairs” and is appropriate only if the requirement is explicitly changed accordingly. Without that change, the result is “No suitable route.”
entries.example: For three routes with stairs, a fallback rule would select the fastest one, while the unchanged requirement calls for the message “No suitable route.”
pitfalls: An additional program rule must not silently change the desired behavior.
entries.heading: Sonderfall: Alle Routen enthalten Treppen

entries.short: A tie occurs when at least two suitable routes have the same duration.
entries.explanation: When durations are equal, duration alone does not determine a unique selection. The requirement must therefore specify which of the equally fast routes to return.
entries.example: A and C are both suitable and each takes 9 minutes.
pitfalls: Without an additional rule, the selection is ambiguous when durations are equal.
entries.heading: Sonderfall: Gleichstand

entries.short: When durations are equal, the first suitable route in the given order remains selected.
entries.explanation: The algorithm replaces its current selection only when it finds a suitable route with a strictly shorter duration. If the durations are equal, it keeps the current route. This makes the result unambiguous and shows how it depends on the input order.
entries.example: If A and C are both suitable and take 9 minutes, A is selected when it appears before C in the list.
pitfalls: Selecting an equally fast route would violate the rule if it comes after the currently selected route.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Sonderfall: Gleichstand

entries.short: An algorithm is a precise sequence of instructions that solves a task for the intended inputs.
entries.explanation: For the route task, the procedure must check every route according to the same rules and produce a result. Its instructions must cover special cases such as ties and the absence of suitable routes.
entries.example: The route procedure checks the list in order, ignores routes with stairs, and keeps track of the fastest suitable route.
pitfalls: “Choose the best route” is not yet a precise algorithm unless “best” is defined.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Algorithmus mit einer bisher besten Route

entries.short: The notation `best = none` means that no route has been selected yet at the start.
entries.explanation: `best` denotes the storage location for the best suitable route found so far. `none` is a pseudocode value meaning “no route”; it is not a route name. If `best` is still `none` at the end, no suitable route was found.
entries.example: Before checking the first route, `best = none` holds.
pitfalls: Do not interpret `none` as an actual route identifier.
The initial marker must remain distinguishable from every selected route.
related: Best route so far (Bisher beste Route)
Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Algorithmus mit einer bisher besten Route

entries.short: The best route so far is the fastest suitable route among those already checked.
entries.explanation: After each check, the stored selection is the fastest route without stairs in the part of the list seen so far. A faster suitable route replaces the current selection; otherwise, the selection is kept.
entries.example: After A (12 minutes, no stairs) and B (7 minutes, with stairs), A remains the best route so far because B is unsuitable.
pitfalls: The best route so far refers only to routes already checked, not to entries that have not yet been checked.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Algorithmus mit einer bisher besten Route

entries.term: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.short: The procedure checks each route once and updates the stored selection only when it finds a suitable, faster route.
entries.explanation: The procedure finds the fastest route without stairs and handles ties and the absence of a suitable route unambiguously. Start with `best = none`, check each route in the given order, and ignore routes with stairs. Store a suitable route if `best = none`; otherwise, replace the selection only with a strictly faster suitable route. At the end, return `best` or report “No suitable route” if `best = none` remains.
entries.example: For A (12 minutes, no stairs), B (7 minutes, with stairs), and C (9 minutes, no stairs), A is stored first, B is ignored, and then C is stored.
pitfalls: Routes with the same duration do not replace the current selection.
A route with stairs must not replace the stored selection.
entries.heading: Algorithmus mit einer bisher besten Route

entries.term: Walkthrough for A, then B, then C
entries.short: The walkthrough shows how the best route so far changes as the three example routes are checked.
entries.explanation: First, A, which takes 12 minutes and has no stairs, is stored as the first suitable route. B, which takes 7 minutes, is ignored because it has stairs. C is suitable and, at 9 minutes, is faster than A, so C is stored and returned.
entries.example: After A, `best = A`; after B, `best = A` remains; after C, `best = C` holds.
pitfalls: B is not selected despite its shorter duration because it has stairs.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Ablauf für A, dann B, dann C

entries.short: For a single selection at the end, it is enough to check the entire route list once, in order.
entries.explanation: With this approach, each route is considered exactly once, and the best suitable route found so far is updated as the list is checked. At the end, `best` contains the desired selection or indicates that no suitable route was found.
entries.example: For four routes, the procedure checks each route once and then returns the result.
pitfalls: Producing a result after each new route arrives is a different requirement from making a single selection at the end.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
Rescanning the routes seen so far (Erneutes Durchgehen der bisherigen Routen)
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.short: For the runtime analysis, assume that checking and updating each route takes constant work.
entries.explanation: The analysis counts how many routes are checked and treats the work on each individual route as independent of the list size. This makes it possible to compare how the total work grows with the number `n` of routes.
entries.example: If each route is checked once and each check takes the same amount of work, the number of checks is proportional to `n`.
pitfalls: The runtime claims assume that checking and updating each route continues to take constant work.
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.term: Keeping track of the best route so far (Merken der bisher besten Route)
entries.short: If a result is needed after each new route arrives, the stored selection only needs to be updated with that new route.
entries.explanation: The selection from the previous step is carried forward. Each newly arriving route requires only one check, so across `n` routes, a total of `n` routes are checked.
entries.example: After route 1, one route has been checked; after route 2, two in total; and after route 3, three.
pitfalls: This claim concerns repeated queries as routes arrive and assumes that the current selection is stored.
related: Rescanning the routes seen so far
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.short: With constant work per route, Θ(n) describes work that grows in proportion to the number `n` of routes.
entries.explanation: Θ(n) means asymptotically linear runtime. When keeping track of the best route, each of the `n` routes is checked once, so under the runtime assumption, the total work is proportional to `n`.
entries.example: With 100 routes, 100 routes are checked; if the number of routes doubles, the number of checks also doubles.
pitfalls: Θ(n) describes how the amount of work grows, not a specific number of seconds.
related: Keeping track of the best route so far
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.term: Rescanning the routes seen so far
entries.short: With rescanning, the entire list received so far is checked again after each new route arrives.
entries.explanation: After the first route, one route is checked; after the second, two are checked, and so on, up to `n` checks after the last route. The total number of checks is therefore `1 + 2 + … + n`, or `\(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\)`. This approach requires more work than continuously keeping track of the best route so far.
entries.example: For four routes received, a total of `1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10` checks are needed.
pitfalls: Repeated checks occur when the entire list so far is processed again after every new route arrives.
related: Keeping track of the best route so far
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.short: With constant work per route, Θ(n²) describes work that grows in proportion to the square of the number of routes.
entries.explanation: Θ(n²) means asymptotically quadratic runtime. When the list seen so far is checked again and again, the total number of checks is `\(\sum_{k=1}^{n} k = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}\)`, which grows asymptotically like `n²`. This classification applies when the entire list is checked again after each new route arrives.
entries.example: With 4 routes, there are 10 checks; with 100 routes, there are 5050.
pitfalls: Here, Θ(n²) applies to repeated checks after each new route arrives, not to a single selection at the end.
related: Rescanning the routes seen so far
entries.heading: Was spart das Merken der besten Route?

entries.short: AI can suggest a procedure, but it cannot decide what your service should do.
entries.explanation: The route a service selects must be specified as a requirement. AI can write code, explain lines, and suggest tests; people must decide and verify choices such as the tie-breaking rule and whether a fallback rule is allowed.
entries.example: The service must specify whether the first or last route is selected when two routes have the same duration.
pitfalls: A plausible-looking AI suggestion does not replace checking whether it meets the intended requirement.
entries.heading: KI: Was bleibt wichtig zu lernen?

entries.short: Testing runs the program with selected inputs and checks whether the results meet the requirements.
entries.explanation: Tests should cover typical inputs and important special cases. For the route task, these include a tie and the case where no route without stairs exists. Tests show whether the program behaves as expected for the inputs checked.
entries.example: A test with A and C as equally fast routes without stairs checks whether the first route is selected.
pitfalls: Testing only the normal case does not cover ties or the absence of suitable routes.
Existing tests do not automatically prove correctness for every possible input.
entries.heading: KI: Was bleibt wichtig zu lernen?

entries.short: An algorithm is correct if it produces a result that meets the requirement for every valid input.
entries.explanation: For the route task, the algorithm must select the fastest route without stairs, keep the first route when durations are equal, and return the appropriate message if no suitable route exists. Tests check behavior on specific inputs; a correctness argument explains why the procedure produces the required result for every valid input.
entries.example: If all routes have stairs, the message “No suitable route” is correct.
pitfalls: A program can run without errors and still produce an incorrect result.
entries.heading: KI: Was bleibt wichtig zu lernen?

entries.short: Efficiency describes how much work an algorithm requires for an input.
entries.explanation: For the route task, the amount of work is compared by counting the routes checked, assuming constant checking work per route. When queries are repeated, keeping track of the best route takes Θ(n) work, while rescanning the entire list seen so far takes Θ(n²) work.
entries.example: For routes arriving one by one, storing the current selection avoids repeated checks.
pitfalls: A faster runtime does not make a procedure correct if it violates the requirement.
entries.heading: KI: Was bleibt wichtig zu lernen?

entries.short: In Java, concrete program instructions implement the input, storage, and execution of the route procedure.
entries.explanation: The abstract steps are made executable in Java: inputs are read, route values are stored, and the selection rule is implemented. The program can then be run, tested, explained, and fixed when errors occur.
entries.example: A Java program can read each route, check whether it has stairs, and store a suitable, faster route as the current selection.
pitfalls: A correct implementation must follow the same rules as the precise requirement.
related: Algorithm that tracks the best route so far
entries.heading: Ausblick: Umsetzung in Java
